question: A 30-year-old otherwise healthy patient comes in with about 1 week of injection and tearing. Her symptoms started in her right eye and then appeared in her left eye. Her slit lamp exam is shown above. What additional feature would be LEAST likely in this patient?
explanation: This patient's history of acute ocular irritation in one eye followed by the other along with the photograph showing faint corneal opacities are classic for viral conjunctivitis followed by formation of subepithelial infiltrates. Usually associated with adenovirus, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) results in a severe follicular conjunctivitis acutely. About 1-3 weeks after acute infection multifocal subepithelial infiltrates form throughout the cornea and are believed to be a combination of white blood cells and immune-complex deposits. These complexes can result in blurred vision when in the central visual axis and may last for months. Topical steroids may be considered to aide in resolution of visually significant subepithelial infiltrates. EKC can result in either pseudo-membranes or true membranes (the rather trivial distinction being that true membranes bleed when removed). Lympadenopathy, particularly pre-auricular, is common in EKC and can help to make the diagnosis. Numerous facial and eyelid molluscum contagiosum (plus or minus follicular conjunctivitis) in a seemingly healthy patient can be a sign of underlying AIDS. EKC with subepithelial infiltrates, however, is common and not associated with AIDS.

question: Which classic adenoviral syndrome is the only one with significant corneal involvement?
explanation: The majority of adenoviral eye infections presents in one of 3 ways: Simple follicular conjunctivitis. This syndrome is self-limited and without systemic symptoms. Most patients will not even seek care for this type of adenoviral ocular infection. An epithelial keratitis can occur, but it is usually short-lived and mild. Pharyngoconjunctival fever. This is the type of adenoviral infection with prominent systemic symptoms including fever, headache, and a sore throat. Again, any corneal involvement is very mild. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC). This is the only subtype of adenoviral infection with significant corneal involvement. This syndrome is characterized by rapid bilateral involvement, preauricular adenopathy, "pseudomembranes" or true conjunctival membranes, and moderate- to-severe tearing and light sensitivity. Corneal signs can include large cornea erosions and/or multifocal subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs). These SEIs can be so prominent as to obscure vision. Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome is not an adenoviral ocular infection. Extra: Epidemic Keratoconjunctivitis - serotypes 8,19,37 Pharyngoconjunctivitis - serotype 7 Simple follicular conjunctivitis - multiple serotypes.

question: Which of the following clinical findings is commonly found in epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)?

options.B: multifocal subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs) developing within 3 days of onset of symptoms
options.C: fibrin formation in the anterior chamber

explanation: There are many viruses that can cause "viral conjunctivitis" and they are broadly divided into DNA viruses and RNA viruses (see outline below). The DNA viruses more frequently result in vision-threatening forms of ocular inflammation and include adenoviruses. There are 4 classic types of conjunctivitis that are caused by different adenovirus serotypes: • Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) • Pharyngoconjunctival fever (PCF) • Acute nonspecific follicular conjunctivitis • Chronic keratoconjunctivitis The causes are: simple follicular conjunctivitis (multiple serotypes), pharyngoconjunctival fever (most commonly serotype 3 or 7), and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC; usually serotype 8, 19, or 37, and subgroup D). Clinically, the syndromes are indistinguishable in the early period. Adenoviral follicular conjunctivitis is not associated with systemic symptoms. Pharyngoconjunctival fever is associated with flu-like symptoms: fever, pharyngitis, and preauricular adenopathy. Adenoviral follicular conjunctivitis and pharyngoconjunctival fever generally don't have epithelial keratitis. EKC causes the most severe form of adenoviral conjunctivitis. 7-10 days after inoculation, patients develop a severe follicular conjunctivitis and punctate keratitis. The conjunctival inflammation ranges from mild inflammation and a mixed follicular/papillary reaction to a severe reaction with subconjunctival hemorrhage, true and pseudomembranes. Keratitis (i.e. corneal inflammation) does not always occur in EKC, but if it does, can be classified into stages: • Stage 0: minute punctate opacities within the corneal epithelium (barely perceptible); within ~2 days of onset. • Stage 1: more easily-observed punctate epithelial keratitis (both with and without fluorescein staining). • Stage 2: coalescence of these lesions and involvement of the deep epithelium ("coarse PEK"). • Stage 3: faint subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs) appear beneath the coarse PEK; typically during 2nd week. • Stage 4: "classic SEIs" (i.e. very easily-observed, multifocal SEIs); typically during 3rd week. • Stage 5: "punctate epithelial granularity" adjacent to and distinct from the SEIs Patients develop multifocal subepithelial infiltrates about 7-14 days after ocular symptoms start. Therapy is supportive and steroids should only be used if there is vision threatening subepi infiltrates or conjunctival membranes. Steroids can prolong the course of the disease and some patients may need them permanently once started. NSAIDs don't help the subepi infiltrates. Patients are considered infectious if they are still hyperemic and tearing. • DNA viruses commonly causing conjunctivitis o Adenovirus o Herpes simplex virus o Varicella-zoster virus o Epstein-Barr virus o Cytomegalovirus o Variola and vaccinia virus o Molluscum contagiosum virus • RNA viruses commonly causing conjunctivitis o Picornaviruses o Paramyxoviruses o Togaviruses o Flaviviruses.

options.C: removal of membranes by forceps to prevent entropion
options.D: use of steroid prophylactically before there are any corneal changes to prevent central corneal opacity

explanation: Steroids should, in general, never be used with infectious processes. They should not be used routinely with adenoviral infections. Other measures that help with adenoviral conjunctivitis include artificial tears and cool compresses, removal of membranes by forceps to prevent entropion, and use of steroid to prevent central corneal opacity (but never prophylactically).

question: Which of the following is a recommended treatment for a patient presenting with recent-onset, herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO)?

options.A: acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day for 14-21 days if the patient is immunocompetent
options.B: trifluridine eyedrops 9x/day until resolution of a pseudodendrite
options.C: topical amitriptyline to prevent post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN)
options.D: intravenous acyclovir if the patient is immunocompromised

explanation: The term "herpes zoster ophthalmicus" (HZO) is typically reserved for varicella zoster virus (VZV) reactivation involving the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (i.e. CN V1). Patients with HZO present characteristically with vesicular lesions involving the upper eyelid and forehead area. These patients may initially complain of a prodrome of fever, malaise, and warmth and a vague uncomfortable sensation in the affected dermatome. According to the BCSC, ocular involvement occurs in >70% of HZO patients and inflammation can occur within any ocular tissue. Some examples of characteristic ocular findings in HZO include: • Conjunctival injection (e.g. papillary or follicular reaction) • Pseudomembrane formation, conjunctival scarring • Episcleritis, anterior or posterior scleritis • punctate epithelial keratitis, pseudodendrites, anterior stromal infiltrates • neurotrophic keratopathy (typically later) • keratitis, endotheliitis • anterior/posterior uveitis • sectoral iris atrophy Management of the acute manifestations of HZO typically includes: 1. Systemic antiviral therapy. For non-immunocompromised patients, the typical regimen is oral valacyclovir 1 gram tid OR acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day OR famciclovir 500 mg tid for a 7-10 day course. Systemic antivirals have been demonstrated to reduce viral shedding from the skin lesions, reduce the chance of systemic dissemination of the virus, and decrease the incidence and severity of the ocular complications. In addition, if begun within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms, systemic antivirals may also decrease the duration of any postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) that occurs later. However, systemic antivirals have not been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of PHN from developing. 2. Any ocular inflammation is treated with topical steroids and cycloplegics. Topical antivirals are typically NOT used for ocular involvement in HZO. 3. The skin lesions are typically treated with a topical antibiotic ointment (e.g. erythromycin) to prevent a bacterial skin superinfection. Warm moist compresses are used for comfort. 4. For immunocompromised patients, intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8hr) is administered to prevent these patients from developing disseminated disease (e.g. encephalitis). 5. Oral steroids are sometimes used by some physicians to help with early zoster pain. However, their use remains controversial at this time. Most acute zoster pain can be treated adequately with oral analgesics. The main overall morbidity from herpes zoster is due to post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) which is commonly defined as the skin pain or dysethesia that occurs >30 days from the date of onset of the attack. The management for PHN is beyond the scope of this question, but some typical therapies include: oral gabapentin (brand: Neurontin), pregabalin (brand: Lyrica), amitriptyline, and capsaicin cream. Answer choice "A" is wrong since the recommended duration of oral antivirals is typically 7-10 days. Answer choice "B" is incorrect since topical antivirals are not typically used for ocular involvement in HZO. Answer choice "C" is incorrect since oral (not topical) amitriptyline may be associated with a decreased duration of PHN if given early in the course of disease and continued until pain symptoms remit. Other notes: The ophthalmic division (i.e. CN V1) further divides into the nasociliary, frontal, and lacrimal branches. It is actually the frontal branch that is most commonly involved in herpes zoster infections. However, involvement of the nasociliary branch confers a higher risk of ocular involvement. This is due to the extensive innervations of the nasociliary nerve with the eye (e.g. conjunctiva, sclera, cornea, iris, and choroid). The lacrimal branch is least commonly affected by HZV. As you probably know, "Hutchinson's sign" describes when vesicles are present on the side of the tip of the nose. This sign indicates infection of the nasociliary nerve and thus a higher likelihood of ocular involvement by HZV.

question: A 10-year-old child presents with a red eye for the previous four months. On your exam, you note a follicular conjunctivitis. He also has the skin lesions seen in the photo above. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this child's presentation?
explanation: These 1-2 mm "umbilicated", dome-shaped, skin-colored papules are classic for molluscum contagiosum which is caused by a DNA poxvirus called "molluscum contagiosum virus" (MCV). MCV is spread via direct contact with infected individuals. Typically, these nodules involve the eyelid margin, but occasionally can be found on the conjunctiva itself. MCV is one of the common causes of chronic follicular conjunctivitis and is thought to be caused by shedding of virus particles from the eyelid (or conjunctival) nodule. Other causes of chronic follicular conjunctivitis include: inclusion conjunctivitis (Chlamydia), trachoma (Chlamydia), and toxic follicular conjunctivitis (e.g. glaucoma drops, antiviral drops). Spontaneous resolution can occur, but is oftentimes prolonged on the order of months to years. Faster recovery can be achieved by excision of the offending lesions, cryotherapy, or incision of the central portion of the lesion. One last high-yield pearl is that extensive molluscum lesions should prompt a workup for HIV infection.

explanation: The systemic manifestations of CRS are deafness (most common systemic sign), cardiac malformations (e.g. patent ductus arteriosus), and ocular findings. Of the possible ocular findings, pigmentary retinopathy is the most common in CRS. Despite the striking appearance of the fundus, vision is not typically affected by this pigmentary retinopathy. Instead, poor vision in CRS is usually caused by cataract and microphthalmos. The classic teaching is that cataract and glaucoma do not occur simultaneously in CRS. question: A prostitute brings her 10-year-old son to be examined by you in the office.  He has been experiencing difficulty seeing and eye irritation.  On exam he has mulberry molars and a saddle nose.  You examine his right eye first and notice interstitial keratitis and "salmon patch" vascularization.  What is the chance that he will have involvement of the left eye as well?
explanation: Syphilitic interstitial keratitis (IK) typically presents late in the first decade of life and represents an immune-mediated manifestation of congenital syphilis. Other nonocular signs of congenital syphilis include: • dental deformitis (e.g. notched incisors and "mulberry molars") • saddle nose, saber shins, frontal bossing, perforation of the palate • deafness • mental retardation Congenital syphilitic IK usually presents bilaterally in 80% of cases although there may be asymmetry in the degree to which each eye is affected. The typical clinical progression of this disease entity is: • Initial symptoms of pain, tearing, photophobia, and perilimbal injection • Sectoral superior stromal inflammation and keratic precipitates seen early • Deep stromal neovascularization occurs later. This stromal vascularization can be intense enough to turn the cornea pink ("salmon patch"). • Inflammation spreads centrally and corneal opacification and edema develop • Corneal scarring and thinning with ghost vessels.

question: You see a patient in clinic with a pigmented conjunctival lesion.  You do an excisional biopsy and the results come back with the diagnosis of conjunctival melanoma.  Which of the following factors does not worsen the prognosis?
explanation: Conjunctival nevi generally present in the first or second decade of life. Limbal nevi tend to be flat while nevi of the bulbar conjunctiva, plica semilunaris, and caruncle tend to be raised. The color can vary from light brown to amelanotic. Approximately 50% contain epithelial inclusion cysts. Observation is generally recommended. Excision should be considered if growth occurs. Benign nevi are rarely found on the palpebral conjunctiva. Therefore, these lesions should always be biopsied if they are found on the palpebral conjunctiva, tarsal conjunctiva, the caruncle, plica semilunaris, or in the fornix. Complexion-associated melanosis (also called racial melanosis or benign acquired melanosis (BAM)) is more associated with persons of darker complexions. It presents with pigmented patches more noticeable near the limbus. It generally is generally bilateral and fairly symmetrical and occurs in adulthood. Primary acquired melanosis (PAM) is generally unilateral and highly asymmetric. It is generally non-cystic. It most often occurs in light-skinned individuals in middle age. Factors that increase risk of progression include: more than 3 clock hours of conjunctival pigmentation, or those involving the caruncle, fornix, or palpebral conjunctiva. Involvement of more than 2 clock hours is an indication for removal. Cellular atypia is the most important factor for predicting progression. PAM without atypia rarely turns malignant and can be followed every 6-12 months. PAM with mild atypia should be monitored more closely. PAM with moderate to severe atypia has a high risk of progression and every effort should be made to remove the entire pigmented conjunctival lesion. If the lesion is too large for removal, topical Mmitomycin C can be used. Conjunctival melanoma generally occurs in middle to late adulthood. It is often nodular and vascular. The overall mortality rate is 25%. They are most commonly found in the bulbar conjunctiva or limbus. About 25% are amelanotic. The origin of melanoma is from PAM (70%), nevus (5%), and de novo (25%). Conjunctival melanomas have a greater than 50% rate of recurrence. Factors that portend a poor prognosis include: • location in the palpebral conjunctiva, caruncle, eyelid margin, or fornix • invasion into deeper tissues • thickness greater than 1.8 mm • pagetoid or full-thickness intraepithelial spread • lymphatic invasion • mixed cell type • de novo origin (i.e. not starting out as PAM or nevus) • tumors not involving the limbus • residual involvement at the surgical margin Excisions of pigmented lesions should include a 2 mm uninvolved margin and avoidance of touching the pigmented area of the lesion when handling to prevent seeding (i.e. "no touch" technique). Incisional biopsies should be avoided because they can spread tumor cells.

question: Which of the following is TRUE about ocular melanocytosis:

explanation: It is secondary to a focal proliferation of subepithelial melanocytes. Because ocular melanocytosis involves pigmentation of the episclera and not the conjunctiva, it is not mobile. About one half of patients with ocular melanocytosis have ipsilateral dermal melanocytosis (Nevus of Ota) and a proliferation of dermal melanocytes in the periocular skin of V1 and V2. Approximately 10% of ocular melanocytosis patients develop glaucoma. The risk of uveal (not conjunctival) melanoma in patients with ocular melanocytosis is 1:400 which is much greater than the sporadic risk in the general population. Only 5% of cases of ocular melanocytosis are bilateral.

question: Which of the following is true concerning primary acquired melanosis (PAM) versus benign melanosis (aka ocular [racial] melanosis)?

options.C: Primary acquired melanosis (PAM) with atypia is associated with malignant potential while benign melanosis is not
options.D: Primary acquired melanosis generally occurs in a bilateral fashion

explanation: Primary acquired melanosis (PAM) is an acquired pigmentation of the conjunctival epithelium (see image below). It is typically unilateral and more commonly seen in fairer- pigmented individuals (e.g. Caucasians) during middle-age (e.g. 50's). PAM is typically a flat, patchy or diffuse brown lesion. PAM is considered a pre-malignant lesion and there are reports that PAM with atypia can progress to conjunctival melanoma in approximately 30-50% of cases. Only biopsy can establish whether atypia is present with these lesions. If PAM is located on the palpebral conjunctiva, fornix, plica, or caruncle, then it is considered more suspicious for having atypia Benign melanosis (aka ocular [racial] melanosis) refers to the increasing conjunctival pigmentation that begins to occur in middle-aged individuals with dark skin (e.g. African Americans). This pigmentation typically occurs in the limbal and perilimbal conjunctival epithelium and sometimes can extend onto the peripheral cornea ("striate melanokeratosis"). As its name implies, benign melanosis does not typically lead to malignant transformation.

question: Which of the following is an acceptable treatment for conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN)?

options.B: surgical excision with 0.5 mm margins and cryotherapy to bordering conjunctiva

explanation: CIN (conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia) typically begins at the limbus and consists of dysplastic cells involving a varying amount of the epithelial layer. These dysplastic cells do not penetrate the basement membrane. The standard treatment for CIN is complete surgical excision of the lesion with 3-4 mm margins and cryotherapy to the bordering conjunctiva. Newer alternatives include topical interferon-alpha2b, mitomycin-C (MMC), and 5- fluorouracil eyedrops (5-FU). Of these three medications, interferon-alpha-2b is gaining the most popularity given its low side effect profile and tolerability compared to MMC or 5-FU. There is some evidence that interferon-alpha-2b alone is as efficacious compared to surgical management of CIN, at least in terms of rates of recurrence (e.g. Ophthalmology. 2014;121:994-1000). Last points: • Cyclosporine drops (e.g. Restasis) are not indicated for this disease. • Topical acetylcysteine is used to treat filamentary keratitis. • Topical bevacizumab can be used to treat graft rejection, neovascularization, and other conditions. There are a few case reports of its use in CIN (e.g. Cornea. 2014;33:1205-9), but it is definitely not as widely used as interferon. • Remember that if you see CIN in a young person, order an HIV panel.

explanation: This is a picture of pyogenic granuloma. Pyogenic granuloma is a reactive hemangioma. It is a misnomer because it is neither infectious nor does it have giant cells. It contains fibroblasts and proliferating capillaries. Histologically, it has a "spoke- wheel" vascular pattern. They are smooth, red, and pedunculated (elongated stalk of tissue). In Ophthalmology, they generally occur after pterygium removal or strabismus surgery. Treatment is with topical or intralesional steroids. If this doesn't work, the lesion can be removed with cautery to the base and frequent post-operative steroids. Foreign body granuloma. It can occur after strabismus surgery, typically over the muscle's reattachment site. It is a localized, elevated, hyperemic, tender mass. It was more common in the past when sutures were made from gut. They often respond to topical steroids but may need surgical excision if they persist. Below is an example of a foreign body granuloma. Please note that a foreign body granuloma and pyogenic granuloma do not generally look at all alike. The pyogenic granuloma is a vascularized tissue that is very red. The foreign body granuloma is a chronic disease process that is mildly red in appearance.

question: The lesion seen in the photo is more likely to be dysplastic or carcinomatous when associated with which of the following HPV subtypes?
explanation: Sessile papillomas occur most commonly at the limbus. They are flat with corkscrew vessels. They have the appearance of a strawberry. When associated with HPV 16 + 18 + 33, sessile conjunctival papillomas are more likely to be dysplastic or carcinomatous. Signs of dysplasia include leukoplakia and symblepharon formation. Pedunculated conjunctival papillomas are associated with HPV 6 + 11 (in children) and HPV 16 (in adults). They have a fibrovascular core and grow out from the surface of their underlying structure from a stalk. It most commonly arises from the inferior fornix. They can proliferate in immunocompromised patients. They generally can be observed. Complete excision with cryotherapy to the base is the preferred removal method. Incomplete excision can lead to proliferation.

question: Which of the following statements about Kaposi's sarcoma is false:

options.B: secondary to a proliferation of vascular epithelium

explanation: It is secondary to a malignant transformation of vascular endothelium.

question: Which of the following risk factors has the worst prognosis in conjunctival melanoma?

options.C: complete excision of the lesion with 4 mm margins
options.D: complete excision of the lesion with 2 mm margins

explanation: Conjunctival melanomas occur most commonly in patients of European ancestry (i.e. Caucasians). The mortality rate from conjunctival melanoma is 25%, which is better than that from uveal or cutaneous melanoma. Conjunctival melanomas most commonly (70%) arise from pre-exisiting primary acquired melanosis (PAM) lesions. Characteristics of conjunctival melanomas that portend an especially bad prognosis include those arising de novo, melanomas not involving the limbus, and residual tumor at the surgical margins after exision.

question: A 65-year-old patient presents to your clinic because he was referred to your clinic for an "eye condition" by his primary care doctor.  He notes an eye growth for the past 6 months, but no changes in his vision or any eye pain.  He has a past medical history of a kidney transplant 20 years ago.  One of the medications that he takes is azathioprine (i.e. Imuran).  On exam, you note the conjunctival lesion seen above.  What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

options.A: basal cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva
options.B: squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva

explanation: tients who are immunosuppressed are much more likely to develop cancers. This includes people that have HIV/AIDS, people with autoimmune conditions, and exposure to tobacco and tar. This particular patient has developed an ocular lesion in the setting of immunosuppression for a kidney transplant. It is well-documented that solid organ transplant recipients are much more likely to develop non-melanoma skin cancers and lymphomas. Specifically they are 65x more likely to develop squamous cell carcinoma and 10x more likely to develop basal cell carcinoma. Increased incidence of squamous cell carcinoma is particularly associated with azathioprine (Imuran) as was the case with this patient. Lymphoma has an increased incidence as well, but not to the magnitude of squamous cell carcinoma. Phlyctenules are not associated with autoimmune diseases. Azathiopurine (Imuran) is a purine nucleoside analog. It prevents DNA replication and RNA transcription. It has been shown to be effective in the treatment of Adamantiades- Behcet uveitis, intermediate uveitis, VKH, sympathetic ophthalmia, and necrotizing scleritis. Initial symptoms after starting the drug include nausea and vomiting. CBCs and liver function tests need to be obtained every 4-6 weeks to watch for bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity. Thiopurine s-methyltransferase (TPMT) breaks down azathioprine. If there is a genetic defect in this gene, azathioprine levels can reach toxic levels and lead to bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity. A new genetic test can screen for patients with these defects. This was a personal patient of mine who had biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva. Recommended treatment is resection of lesion with 4 mm margins, thin lamellar scleral flap under the lesion, treatment of the remaining sclera with absolute alcohol, and cryotherapy to the remaining conjunctival margins. Also of note, this patient had hundreds of squamous cell carcinomas of his skin removed by his dermatologist. So, referral to a dermatologist would be prudent in any patient with a conjunctival squamous cell carcinoma for a full body skin check.

question: Which of the following steps should be done first in the repair of an open globe?
explanation: The BCSC Cornea book outlines specific steps in the repair of an open globe: 1. Induction of general anesthesia. Though there are some studies promoting the alternative of MAC/local anesthesia, general anesthesia is preferred in most circumstances especially if there is prolapse of uveal tissue through scleral lacerations. The rationale underlying using general anesthesia (and not retro- or peribulbar blocks) is that general anesthesia will not increase orbital pressure which could lead to expulsion of additional intraocular contents. 2. Excision of anteriorly prolapsed vitreous; removing lens fragments; removing corneal foreign bodies. 3. If any prolapsed uveal tissue or retina is seen, it should be gently reposited back into the eye. The surgeon should use a gentle sweeping motion through a separate limbal incision, with the aid of viscoelastics to reform the anterior chamber. One should try to preserve as much uveal/retinal tissue as is possible. Uveal tissue should only be cut or removed if it is frankly necrotic or infected. Any epithelial tissue that has migrated into the eye should be removed if it can be safely done. 4. Repair the corneal limbus first. The corneal limbus serves as a good landmark to begin repair which will aid in restoring the rest of the globe to its original anatomical condition. Typically, this initial repair is done with a 9-0 nylon suture. 5. Repair the rest of any corneal laceration(s). Typically, this is accomplished with 10-0 nylon sutures. Longer "compression" suture throws are used in the peripheral cornea while shorter suture throws are used in the central cornea. This technique helps to reform the natural curvature of the cornea (i.e. steeper centrally). To prevent incarceration of iris tissue, some surgeons will throw "shallower" suture passes until a watertight closure is achieved. Then any iris tissue is swept away from the posterior cornea (e.g. with a cyclodialysis spatula). Then these shallow sutures are replaced with "ideal", near full- thickness sutures. The surgeon should bury the knots into the corneal stroma and not the wound. 6. Repair of any scleral laceration is then performed in an anterior-to-posterior direction in an interrupted fashion (e.g. with 9-0 or 8-0 nylon). During this repair, any prolapsed vitreous again should be cut flush with the globe's surface and uveal/retinal tissue gently reposited back into the eye.

question: In general, what is the maximum time that you can wait to enucleate an eye after an open globe injury before increasing your risk for sympathetic ophthalmia (SO)?
explanation: The general consensus in the Ophthalmology community is that an enucleation should be performed within 2 weeks of a ruptured globe injury to decrease the risk of sympathetic ophthalmia occurring in the uninjured eye. However, SO has been reported to occur as soon as 5 days and as late as 66 years after the initial injury. Despite this, SO is a very rare entity, with an estimated incidence of 0.2% after nonsurgical trauma. Extra: Disease Entity and History Sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) is a rare, bilateral, granulomatous uveitis caused by exposure of previously immune-privileged ocular antigens from trauma or surgery with a subsequent bilateral autoimmune response to this tissue. The injured or operated eye is the exciting eye and the contralateral eye is the sympathizing eye. Clinical evaluation This fundus image of a patient with sympathetic ophthalmia demonstrates vitritis and a multifocal choroiditis. Sympathetic ophthalmia is characterized by inflammation involving any part and most of the uveal tract. Anterior segment findings include keratic precipitates, anterior chamber reaction, posterior synechiae and the development of a cataract. In eyes with chronic inflammation, either elevated pressures from inflammatory glaucoma or hypotony from ciliary body shutdown can develop. Posteriorly, patient can develop vitritis, papillitis, multifocal choroiditis, Dalen- Fuchs nodules, multiple exudative retinal detachments, macular edema, choroidal neovascularization and epiretinal membranes Sympathetic Ophthalmia : Rare, bilateral, diffuse granulomatous uveitis made up of lymphocytic infiltration of the uveal tract with nests of epithelioid cells Occurs a few days to several decades after penetrating accidental or surgical trauma to an eye Both the “exciting” (traumatized) and “sympathizing” (fellow) eye are affected Clinical signs and symptoms are usually detected within the first 3 months after trauma with the peak incidence 4 to 8 weeks after trauma Signs and symptoms in the sympathizing eye are variable and may be subtle Posterior segment findings include papillitis, generalized retinal edema, and small yellow-white deposits beneath the retinal pigment epithelium (Dalen-Fuchs nodules) Fluorescein angiography typically shows multiple fluorescing dots at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium in the venous phase which persist (also seen in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome) In eyes with very poor visual potential and demonstrated disorganization of the ocular contents, enucleation within 2 weeks of injury is advised to prevent the disease Enucleation of the exciting eye after the development of sympathetic ophthalmia is controversial and not shown to be of benefit High dose steroids are the mainstay of therapy once the disease is present and should be continued for at least 6 months after the resolution of inflammation.

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the management of a hyphema?

options.B: the patient should continue normal activity
options.C: cycloplegics are useful to reduce eye pain

explanation: Most eye physicians will advise patients with traumatic hyphemas to avoid anti-clotting medications like aspirin or warfarin to expedite clotting and also to reduce the risk of rebleeding. It is also prudent to keep the patient's head elevated so that gravity can help in the resolution of the hyphema. Most physicians would also provide a strong cycloplegic, like atropine, to decrease ocular discomfort from ciliary muscle spasm. Though there is prospective data supporting the use of oral antifibrinolytic medications (e.g. Amicar = aminocaproic acid) to prevent rebleeds, these medications have failed to demonstrate a superior visual benefit compared to standard therapy. In addition, many patients will not tolerate these oral medications due to their significant side effects (e.g. nausea, postural hypotension, and arrhythmias). Their high side effect profile limits their use.

question: Which of the following is an indication to perform an anterior chamber washout to remove a hyphema?

options.A: Intraocular pressure (IOP) greater than 35 mmHg for 2 days with a microhyphema (no clot inferiorly)
options.B: Intraocular pressure (IOP) greater than 25 mmHg for 7 days with a microhyphema (no clot inferiorly)
options.C: Intraocular pressure (IOP) greater than 25 mmHg for 1 day in a patient with sickle cell disease
options.D: Normal intraocular pressure (IOP), but a 30% blood clot for greater than 2 weeks

explanation: A 30% blood clot is not a threat to vision. An anterior chamber washout can reduce the occurrence of optic atrophy secondary to high IOP. Indications for washout include: IOP greater than 60 mmHg for 2 days, IOP greater than 35 mmHg for 7 days, and IOP greater than 25 mmHg for 1 day in a patient with sickle cell disease. You would also want to washout the AC at the first signs of corneal blood staining.

question: A 14-year-old African American boy is hit by a baseball in the right eye.  His ocular exam is significant for a 40% hyphema and an intraocular pressure of 30 mmHg in the right eye.  His past medical history is only significant for sickle cell trait.  Which of the following medications would you want to avoid using in this patient?
explanation: It is recommended to obtain a sickle cell workup in an African American patient who presents with a traumatic hyphema. The reason is that patients with sickle cell disease or sickle cell trait are predisposed to sickling of the red blood cells (RBCs) in the anterior chamber. These sickled RBCs have a harder time draining through the trabecular meshwork and thus can lead to very high intraocular pressures (IOPs) with even a small hyphema. Also, the optic nerves of these individuals may be more susceptible to damage with even slight IOP elevations due to diminished optic nerve blood flow. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g. acetazolamide) and osmotic agents (e.g. mannitol) lead to a lowered pH in both the bloodstream and anterior chamber as well as dehydration. Both of these effects can precipitate a sickle cell crisis and/or worsened drainage of the RBCs through the trabecular meshwork.

question: In general, which of the following is more likely to cause a decrease in vision?
explanation: Surface irregularities decrease vision to a greater degree than stromal changes. Extra: possibly because the air/corneal interface is where most of the refracting power comes from.

question: You complete a cataract surgery (that had a moderate amount of phaco time) and cannot tell whether you have broken the posterior capsule. The patient is sent home. On his post-operative day 1 visit, you note that the anterior chamber is 80% filled with vitreous and is covering 80% of the endothelium. There is 2+ stromal edema and the intraocular pressure is 30 mmHg in this eye. Which of the following is the best management choices for this patient?
explanation: This patient is suffering damage to his corneal endothelium which can be irreversible if not taken care of in a timely manner. The correct management choice is urgent return to the operating room for a thorough anterior vitrectomy to remove all vitreous from the anterior chamber to prevent corneal decompensation as well as intractable glaucoma, cystoid macular edema, and retinal breaks.

question: In the case of recurrent subconjunctival hemorrhage, which of the following should be considered as a potential cause?
explanation: It is rare for a subconjunctival hemorrhage to be associated with an underlying systemic condition. Sometimes, it is associated with severe coughing, Valsalva maneuver, or vomiting. The only time subconjunctival hemorrhages require a systemic workup is if they are recurrent. Some associated systemic diseases include uncontrolled hypertension (not hypotension), bleeding diathesis, and diabetes. Thyroid dysfunction is not associated with recurrent subconjunctival hemorrhages. Homocystinuria is associated with a hypercoaguable state.

question: Which of the following is the most reliable predictor of final visual outcome in traumatized eyes?
explanation: The initial presenting visual acuity is the most reliable predictor of final visual outcome after a traumatic eye injury. Extra: Ocular Trauma Score.

question: You just completed your 40th overall cataract surgery and you think you have done an excellent job. You are about to take out the lid speculum when your instructor tells you to re-examine the cornea. You note a 40% Descemet's membrane tear emanating from the phaco wound. Which of the following is the best treatment option?

options.C: place an air bubble in the anterior chamber
options.D: inject viscoelastic into the anterior chamber overnight

explanation: DSAEK (Descemet's Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty) has taught us that air bubbles are very good at re-approximating Descemet's membrane to stroma. Placing sutures is a good option, but it is not the best due to their tendency to induce scarring and astigmatism.

question: A 28-year-old male patient presents to your clinic with acute right eye pain that has worsened over the last few hours.  He states that for the last week he has been taking care of his neighbors' plants while they were on vacation.  He actually has a picture of these plants (see above).  Which of the following findings might you expect on exam?
explanation: This is a picture of the Dieffenbachia plant. They are common houseplants because they have interestingly colored leaves and a high tolerance for shade which makes them low- maintenance. They contain needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals called raphides. The sap of this plant can get into the eyes and cause an acute keratoconjunctivitis associated with needle- like crystals in the cornea.

question: Which of the following is the most common indication for penetrating keratoplasty (PKP)?
explanation: The three major types of corneal transplantation techniques are the replacement of the anterior cornea, the posterior cornea, or both. For trainees, learning about the different types of corneal surgeries is a little bit like learning about alphabet soup! It may help to arrange them anatomically to help keep the various procedures separate: Anterior Lamellar Procedures 1. ALK/SALK - anterior lamellar keratoplasty or superficial anterior lamellar kertoplasty. This procedure may be used for cases of anterior stromal scarring (eg, HSV scarring or recalcitrant haze) wherein the depth of the opacity is not very deep (~200-300 microns). Anterior segment OCT imaging may be used to measure the depth of the lesion so that as much healthy host corneal tissue can be preserved using only a superficial trephination. Femtosecond laser may be used to more accurately prepare the donor button and incise within the host for more accurate replacement of diseased tissue with healthy tissue (FALK). 2. DALK - deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty. This procedure is used for deep scarring that includes the posterior stromal layers so long as the host DM/endothelial layers are healthy. For example, DALK is an excellent option for keratoconus patients as the DM/endothelium in these patients is usually healthy, and avoiding the transplantation of donor DM/endothelium may lead to lower rejection rates. Posterior Lamellar Procedures 1. DLEK - deep lamellar endothelial keratoplasty. This is somewhat of a historical term as it may be considered as the "grandfather" of EK procedures (early 2000's) (since it went on to father DSAEK/DSAEK which fathered DMEK). In this procedure, a large amount of stromal tissue (~200 microns) was used as a scaffold for donor DM/endothelial tissue 2. DSEK/DSAEK - Descemet's stripping (automated) endothelial keratoplasty was introduced in the mid 2000's as a refinement of the DLEK procedure. With the advent of more precise ways of cutting the donor cornea, lesser amounts of stromal tissue (100-150 microns) was needed as a scaffold for donor DM/endothelial tissue. Both of these procedure are essentially the same; however, in DSEK, the tissue is prepared by a manual dissection method, whereas in DSAEK, the tissue prepared by an automated method that allows for more precise and reproducible desired thickness of the donor tissue. Most donor grafts in the United States at the time of this writing (March 2020) are prepared using the automated method, so it is more accurate to refer to these procedures as DSAEK alone. However, because the term "DSEK" was used by many corneal surgeons prior to the widespread popularity of DSAEK, many surgeons will use "DSEK" nomenclature even though they are referring to DSAEK (confusing, yes!). As if this weren't already complicated enough, recently terms such as "UT-DSAEK (ultrathin DSAEK)" and "nano- thin DSAEK" have been introduced to refer to DSAEK grafts that are <100 microns and <50 microns, respectively. DSAEK remains an excellent choice for eyes that may not have 20/20 vision potential, for patients that may not be able to lay flat for a long period of time, for patients with other ocular pathologies (such as glaucoma tubes, post-vitrectomy, high myopia, aphakia) that may make DMEK more challenging. DSAEK also has a lower detachment and rebubble rate compared to DMEK, which may make it a preferred choice for patients who may not be able to follow up closely. Vision potential with DSAEK, especially UT-DSAEK, is increasingly approaching 20/30-20/25. As a result, some surgeons are preferring UT-DSAEK or NT-DSAEK as their EK procedure of choice. 3. PDEK - Pre-Descemet's endothelial keratoplasty was introduced as a means to transplant as little stromal tissue as possible. In this technique, the big bubble technique that is used in DALK is used to create a donor graft that consists of extreme posterior stroma (Dua's layer), DM and endothelium. PDEK grafts are about ~30 microns. It is thought that this amount of minimal stromal tissue allows for some ease of manipulation inside the eye and lower rates of detachment. Very few corneal surgeons perform PDEK as both DSAEK and DMEK are relatively easy to perform with proper patient selection. 4. DMEK - Descemet's membrane endothelial keratoplasty is the logical conclusion for EK procedures. In this surgery, the host DM/endothelium is replaced by a layer of donor DM/endothelium (~10-15 microns) for a true 1:1 replacement of diseased tissue with healthy tissue. DMEK is increasingly become the procedure of choice for EK for eyes that have 20/20 vision potential, such as Fuch's endothelial dystrophy. While DMEK may have slightly higher risks for detachment and rebubbling, DMEK vision potential (both objective and subjective) remains the highest among all existing corneal transplant procedures. 5. DSO/DWEK - Descemet's stripping only or Descemetorrhexis without endothelial keratoplasty is a relatively new procedure that remains early in its experimental phase and remains highly controversial. In this procedure, the central 4 mm of guttae are removed (therefore only applicable to eyes with guttae in the central 4 mm of the visual axis) and no donor corneal tissue is placed. The rationale is that surrounding endothelial cells will slide in from the periphery after surgery and will eventually clear the cornea, which may take up to 3 months to occur. Patients are concurrently placed on a Rho-kinase inhibitor (which is not FDA approved, Rispasudil) to help prevent endothelial cell apoptosis and stimulate endothelial migration. Short-term results appear to be promising, but long-term results remain to be seen. One problem remains that even if the peripheral cells slide in, these cells have the same apoptotic genetic defect that will lead to guttae/eventual cell death in the future. Full Thickness Procedures When all layers are transplanted, it is referred to as PKP or PK (penetrating keratoplasty). By far, the most common indication for PKP is keratoconus followed by regraft (for failed PKP) and then other forms of corneal scarring (HSV or ulcer scarring, etc.) The percentage of all transplants that are PKPs has dramatically decreased from 95% in 2005 to 42% in 2014. In contrast, endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK and DMEK) percentages of all transplants have increased from 3% in 2005 to 56% in 2014. In 2014, DSAEK represented 49.7% of all transplants and DMEK represented 6.2% of all transplants. However, the percentage of DMEK transplants is rising as surgeons are becoming more comfortable with the technique. In 2014, anterior lamellar transplants (ALK, DALK, and FALK) represented about 2.0% of total transplants.

question: Which of the following conditions is most amenable to deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK)?
explanation: DALK involves the removal of the corneal epithelium and stroma leaving behind the host endothelium. This procedure should only be undertaken in patients with normal corneal endothelium (e.g. Reis-Bucklers, which is a dystrophy affecting Bowman's layer). All of the other conditions involve the corneal endothelium and are therefore more amenable to endothelial keratoplasty techniques (e.g. DSAEK and DMEK).

question: Which of the following is the most common indication for corneal transplant in children?
explanation: Peters anomaly is a central defect in Descemet's membrane with absence of endothelium resulting in a cloudy central cornea. Peters is in the differential diagnosis of a cloudy cornea at birth. This differential diagnosis can be remembered by the mnemonic "STUMPED": • Sclerocornea • Trauma • Ulcer • Mucopolysaccharidoses • Peters anomaly • Endothelial (e.g. CHED) • Dermoid Of these, Peters is the most common indication for corneal transplant in children. Peters anomaly is due to the "localized absence of corneal endothelium and Descemet's membrane underneath a central corneal opacity." It is generally inherited sporadically. If inherited bilaterally, a genetic workup should be undertaken. Per BCSC Cornea, it is bilateral in 80% of patients. Glaucoma occurs in 50% of cases. Aniridia, PFV, retinal detachment, and microcornea can also occur along with Peters anomaly. Peters anomaly type 1 is characterized by iridocorneal adhesions in the area of the nonvascularized corneal opacity. It is associated with mutations in PITX2, FOXC1, CYP1B1, PAX6, and other genes. Peters anomaly type 2 is the occurrence of lens touch to the area of the vascularized corneal opacity. It is due to a failure of the lens vesicle to separate from the surface ectoderm. It is due to mutations in the gene FOXE3. Peters plus syndrome includes Peters anomaly along with systemic defects. Systemic defects can include congenital brain defect, heart defects, and craniofacial anomalies (along with others).

question: Which of the following is associated with cornea/lenticular touch with an overlying vascularized cornea?
explanation: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome (AR), also known as mesodermal dysgenesis, is a group of congenital anterior segment defects that lead to glaucoma in 50% of cases. It is often autosomal dominant and is associated with mutations in the PITX2 gene. In AR, there is always a prominent Schwalbe's line (posterior embryotoxon). Other ocular signs include: corectopia, iris holes, iridocorneal adhesions, and ectropion uveae. Systemic findings in AR include: maxillary hypoplasia, redundant periumbilical skin, hypospadias, and teeth abnormalities including absent teeth (hypodontia) and small teeth (microdontia). AR is caused by abnormal migration of neural crest cells which are required for the normal development of the anterior segment (among many other things).

question: You are called to the floor for a pediatric consult. You are given the history of a child with a cloudy cornea since birth. You happen to wheel your anterior OCT (optical coherence tomography) machine to the floor and note an absence of Descemet's membrane and endothelium centrally. Curiously, you note the other eye is normal. What percentage of patients with this condition will have it bilaterally?
explanation: This infant's presentation is most likely due to Peters anomaly. The catch phrase for Peters anomaly is the "localized absence of corneal endothelium and Descemet's membrane underneath a central corneal opacity." It is generally inherited sporadically. If inherited bilaterally, a genetic workup should be undertaken. Per BCSC Cornea, it is bilateral in 80% of patients. Glaucoma occurs in 50% of cases. Aniridia, PFV, retinal detachment, and microcornea can also occur along with Peters anomaly. Peters anomaly type 1 is characterized by iridocorneal adhesions in the area of the nonvascularized corneal opacity. It is associated with mutations in PITX2, FOXC1, CYP1B1, PAX6, and other genes. Peters anomaly type 2 is the occurrence of lens touch to the area of the vascularized corneal opacity. It is due to a failure of the lens vesicle to separate from the surface ectoderm. It is due to mutations in the gene FOXE3. Peters plus syndrome includes Peters anomaly along with systemic defects. Systemic defects can include congenital brain defect, heart defects, and craniofacial anomalies (along with others).

question: You are about to suture in a 16 interrupted-suture penetrating keratoplasty (PKP). The placement of which suture contributes the most to post-operative astigmatism?
explanation: The first suture anchors the graft to the bed. But it is the second suture that determines how the graft is going to "fit" in the bed. So after the first suture is placed, it is critical that the surgeon carefully place the second suture so that it is directly opposite the first. This can be done by grasping the tissue with 0.12 forceps opposite of the first suture, stretching the graft so that it is slightly taut, and then slightly moving it side to side over where the surgeon thinks the second suture should go. As the graft is moved slightly side to side, the surgeon can judge if it is directly opposite the first suture by how the graft is overlying the bed on either side of the graft (the areas where the third and fourth sutures will go). Extra: "The second cardinal suture is considered the most important suture in keratoplasty, because it is crucial in determining lateral wound apposition, proper do- nor/recipient edge alignment, and corneal astigmatism."

question: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pKq8b7wSJuc
explanation: The video is demonstrating the technique of Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) which is the iteration of endothelial keratoplasty that has followed Descemet stripping endothelial keratoplatsy (DSEK). DMEK involves transplanting just Descemet membrane and endothelium to the host cornea which has been stripped of diseased endothelium/Descemet membrane. In contrast, DSEK involves transplanting Descemet membrane/endothelium and a small portion of posterior stroma (e.g. a typical DSEK donor graft is ~100 microns thick). A direct comparison study between DMEK and DSEK found better visual acuity results in the former. Specifically, this study showed best-corrected visual acuity to increase from 0.70 ± 0.48 logMAR and 0.75 ± 0.32 logMAR before surgery to 0.17 ± 0.12 logMAR and 0.36 ± 0.15 logMAR 6 months after DMEK and DSAEK respectively (P < .001). (PubMed). This study showed significant differences in endothelial counts at 3 months, but not at 6 months between the two surgical groups. The prevailing theory on why DMEK offers better visual acuity results is that it better mimics the physiological posterior corneal curvature and thus results in lower higher order aberrations and also light scatter. The disadvantages of DMEK that are generally agreed upon are: • Steeper learning curve. While DSEK involves relatively-straightforward graft insertion and unfolding techniques, successful DMEK requires the surgeon to master a series of maneuvers (e.g. "tapping" and "pressing") to help unfold the donor in the correct orientation. • More difficult donor preparation. Given its extreme thinness, it is very easy to tear the DMEK graft as it is peeled off its underling stroma. In addition, successful DMEK requires a "no touch" technique unlike DSEK which is more forgiving given the thickness of the tissue. • Increased surgical times. Both graft preparation and graft unfolding contribute to increased average surgical times compared to DSEK. • Increased rate of graft detachments (and thus air rebubbling rates). • More expensive. This is generally related to precut DMEK tissue which most eye banks will charge more for compared to DSEK tissue. DMEK gets even more expensive if you tear the tissue excessively and have to use a second donor graft!

question: Which of the following factors is MOST strongly associated with an increased immune response in corneal transplants?

options.A: increased production of endostatin (fragment of collagen XVII)
options.B: increased production and secretion of VEGFR-2
options.D: increased production and secretion of VEGF

explanation: The remarkable ability of corneal transplant grafts to escape immune rejection is attributable to numerous anatomical, immunoregulatory and physiological conditions that simultaneously work together to prevent the activation and expression of alloimmunity. This idea of "immune privilege" bears clarification: it does not mean there is an unrestricted exemption from activation of immunological defense mechanisms. Immune privilege is lost in any situation in which chronic inflammation, neovascularization (through increased VEGF, answer choice D), or trauma is present at the ocular surface. Three factors are necessary to establish immune privilege for corneal transplants: 1) Afferent blockade - blocking the inception of the host immune response. Presence of blood vessels in the corneal graft bed not only stimulates an immune response by providing a channel for immune elements to interact with the corneal graft, but also promotes lymphangiogenesis as well. Corneal epithelial and stromal cells secrete a soluble form of VEGFR-2 (answer choice B), which blocks VEGF-C and inhibits lymphangiogenesis in the cornea, but does not affect hemangiogenesis.1 The cornea also produces endostatin2, a proteolytic fragment of collagen XVII (answer choice A), that inhibits both hemangiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis. In corneal transplants, there is decreased production of endostatin and increased production of VEGFR that combine to increase neovascularization and eventual immune rejection. In short, controlling both hemangiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis is necessary for the survival of corneal transplants. 2) Down-regulating the normal immune response to a state of immune tolerance. Corneal transplants (excluding DALK grafts), specifically the transplanted endothelium (in the case of PK and EK grafts), are exposed to the host anterior chamber and are therefore in direct contact with numerous anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive cytokines present in aqueous humor. During and after corneal transplant surgery, corneal antigens from the graft, including all antigenic cells, enter the anterior chamber. T his leads to a unique immune response that will actually down-regulate antigen-specific delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) and favor the production of non-complement-fixing antibodies (answer choice C). If you are still awake, this leads to a phenomenon known as anterior chamber-associated immune deviation (ACAID), which leads to immune privilege and corneal graft survival.3 In addition, there is evidence of a distinct, regulatory T cell (Treg, which rely on cytokines such as IL-17 and are separate from the ACAID pathway) that also favors the survival of corneal grafts. 3) Removing factors that induce immune response in the corneal transplant, especially at the graft-host interface, both on the ocular surface and in the anterior chamber. For example, the cornea contains many molecules that shut off effector response elements, such as T cells and components of the complement pathway. To a lesser degree, corneal grafts can stimulate the generation of antibodies that are also capable of inducing complement-dependent cytolysis of the graft. Furthermore, at the aqueous humor interface, recall that corneal endothelial cells do not express MHC class Ia molecules which are necessary to prevent activation of the NK cells -- think of the MHC class Ia molecule as a legal "permit to reside" that cells must display, otherwise the NK cells will eliminate them immediately. However, there are other molecules in the aqueous humor, such as macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), that downregulate NK cell activity (think of MIF telling the NKs to chillax and calm the frick down). The net result is that the aqueous humor contains elements that inhibit NK cells, both short-term and long-term, and therefore protect the corneal graft from NK-mediated rejection. In summary, a harmonious symphony of mechanisms and molecules work together to establish corneal immune privilege. Immune privilege allows the eye to be shielded from most immune- mediated inflammation, but it also increases the eye's risk for infection. When one considers all the etiologies of infectious blindness (HSV, trachoma, etc), these are really immune-mediated diseases in which immune privilege has been compromised. However, the eye will forego immune privilege when faced with situations in which it determines a significant enough danger, and will therefore choose preservation of life over preservation of vision. When corneal transplants function well, it is because immune privilege (through the mechanisms discussed above) shields the corneal transplant from the eye's defense mechanisms. However, chronic inflammation, neovascularization and trauma may be sufficient to suspend immune privilege, activate immunological defense mechanisms (including neovascularization in a vicious cycle) that lead to the rejection of the corneal graft.

question: A patient of yours who is status post uncomplicated penetrating keratoplasty in the right eye from two months ago presents with an intraocular pressure of 32 mmHg in that eye.  You elect to initiate anti-ocular hypertensive therapy.  Which of the following medications would pose the greatest risk of corneal edema?
explanation: Elevated intraocular pressure is fairly common after penetrating keratoplasty, due to either postoperative inflammation, trabecular meshwork injury, or steroid response. In selecting anti-ocular hypertensive therapy, we must be careful about which agents we initiate. Of the answer choices, topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as dorzolamide are well known to increase the risk of corneal edema and subsequent decompensation. This class of medications inhibits the function of the endothelial Na/K ATPase, an enzyme that maintains corneal deturgescence. Its inhibition predisposes to endothelial cell failure, and ultimate graft failure with corneal edema. WRONG ANSWERS: • Miotics, such as pilocarpine, increase the risk of graft rejection, not edema. This is due to their effect of breaking down the blood-ocular barrier, which increases the influx of immune cells and predisposes to graft rejection. • Prostaglandin analogs are inherently pro-inflammatory, and one could consider avoiding this class of medications in a corneal transplant recipient to avoid increasing the risk of graft rejection. However, they are more classically associated with reactivation of herpetic keratitis. • Beta adrenergic antagonists and alpha-2 adrenergic agonists are relatively well tolerated with the former typically associated with punctate corneal epitheliopathy and the latter with follicular conjunctivitis.

question: In which of the following situations would a penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) with a running suture be most indicated?
explanation: PKP utilizing interrupted sutures is the procedure of choice in thin corneas, vascularized corneas, children, and inflamed corneas. This allows the surgeon to selectively remove sutures if there is vascularization to one area of the graft. If you had a running suture, you would be out of luck. Keratoconus patients actually have some of the longest surviving graft s/p PKP.

question: A 48-year-old patient presents to your office with worsening vision over the past 3 days in the right eye.  His past ocular history is significant for a penetrating keratoplasty of the right eye that was performed for keratoconus 5 years ago.  Slit-lamp exam of the right eye is shown above.  These exam findings are most consistent with which of the following processes?
explanation: The faint, gray line seen in the photo is classic for a Khodadoust line, which is a wave of endothelial keratic precipitates (KP) marching across the endothelial surface. This line of KP is a hallmark of endothelial graft rejection, which is the most common type of corneal graft rejection. The Khodadoust line damages the endothelium and thus leaves stromal edema in its "wake" as it progresses across the graft. There are 4 main types of graft rejection which correspond to different layers of the cornea: • Epithelial rejection. This type of rejection is seen in approximately 10% of patients experiencing a rejection episode. It typically occurs in the earlier post-operative period (1 to 13 months) since the donor epithelium is eventually replaced by the host epithelium in older grafts. Since the donor epithelium lost in an epithelial rejection episode can be replaced with host epithelium, epithelial rejection itself does not cause long-term problems. However, it may herald the onset of endothelial rejection which can lead to permanent damage to the graft. Epithelial rejection manifests as an elevated, linear ridge that advances centripetally. This epithelial rejection line can be distinguished from a Khodadoust line since there is no associated stromal edema with an epithelial rejection line. • Subepithelial rejection. Graft rejection can also take the form of subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs) which resemble the SEIs seen in epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. It accounts for approximately 10-15% of rejection episodes. These SEIs are 0.2-0.5 mm in diameter and occur only in the donor tissue. Like epithelial rejection, subepithelial rejection itself does not cause long-term damage to the graft. However, it is considered an early sign of rejection and again can herald the onset of endothelial rejection. • Stromal rejection. This is the least common form of graft rejection and can be seen as stromal infiltrates, neovascularization, or keratolysis within the graft- host interface. In very severe episodes, stromal rejection can take the form of frank stromal necrosis. • Endothelial rejection. Again, endothelial rejection is the most common type of graft rejection accounting for up to ~40% of episodes. It is also considered the most serious form of graft rejection since endothelial cells lost cannot be replaced. Endothelial rejection can take the form of scattered KP or as a Khodadoust line. There is typically an associated anterior chamber reaction. The mainstay treatment for all forms/episodes of graft rejection is corticosteroids (e.g. topical steroids for mild episodes; subTenon injection for severe episodes or non- compliant patients; or systemic for the worst forms.).

question: Which of the following indications for corneal grafting has the best prognosis for graft survival?
explanation: Keratoconus patients have the best chance of having a successful corneal transplant. The other answer choices are actually risk factors for graft rejection. These risk factors are thought to increase the likelihood of bringing in inflammatory cells that then recognize the foreign corneal tissue.

question: Which of the following past medical histories will allow the use of a potential donor's cornea for Descemet's Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK)?
explanation: DSAEK is a type of corneal transplant that involves replacing the recipient's endothelium with a circular donor lenticle of tissue composed of endothelium and a thin layer of posterior stroma. LASIK does not affect the endothelium and is therefore not a contraindication for DSAEK tissue use. The other choices are contraindications to tissue donation.

question: Which of the following would be an appropriate option for surgical intervention for the right eye?
explanation: This patient likely has a history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome based on his history of extended period of hospitalization secondary to allergic response to trimethoprim- sulfamethoxazole. Corneal transplants in such patients have an extremely guarded prognosis due to the nature of chronic, relentless bilateral inflammation, stem cell deficiency, and neovascularization of the cornea. Endothelial and/or repeat penetrating keratoplasty would have a high risk of failure based on the nature of the disease and response to previous keratoplasties. Cautious observation (ie, no surgery) may be a reasonable choice in clinical practice given the extensive risks associated with further surgery, especially if the patient is pain-free, but it is not given as a choice here. Therefore, a keratoprosthesis (KPro) would be the best choice among the given answers. A type 1 KPro works well in patients with a good blink reflex and moist ocular surface whereas a type 2 KPro would work well in patients with extensive conjunctival scarring, dry eye and poor blink reflex. Other types of keratoprosthesis (TKPro, etc) are available for other high-risk patients.

question: A 67-year-old patient with a previous history of cataract surgery four years ago presents with complaints of blurry vision that is particularly worse upon awakening which improves as the day goes on . Examination is reveals 3+ confluent guttae with admixed corneal edema in both eyes. Visual acuity is 20/60 in both eyes. The previous manifest refraction performed 1 year ago was: OD: -0.25 sph (20/25) OS: -0.25 sph (20/30) Which of the following refractive changes may occur despite successful Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK)?
explanation: Descemet's stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK) is a tissue additive procedure (~50-150 microns) that can cause changes in the power corneal curvature and a subsequent post-operative hyperopic shift, approximately 0.5 to 1.5 D in magnitude. When performing concurrent cataract surgery and DSAEK, corneal surgeons often intentionally target -1 to -1.5 D myopia in order to compensate for the hyperopic shift induced by DSAEK. Currently, DMEK (Descemet's membrane endothelial keratoplasty) is increasing in popularity as a procedure of choice for replacement of diseased endothelium in Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy. DMEK involves a direct, one-to-one replacement of the diseased endothelium/Descemet's membrane with donor endothelium/Descemet's membrane. However, there is still a hyperopic shift that occurs even with this procedure, likely due to muliple reasons, including but not limited to: 1. thinning of the cornea (compared to pre-operative thickness) as a result of corneal deturgescence when compared to the pre-operative thickness 2. change in posterior curvature of the cornea that essentially adds "minus" power to the cornea This patient has a small amount of myopia at this time and may develop hyperopia (up to +1.5D) after DSAEK. It is important to have this discussion with patients prior to any type of endothelial keratoplasty so that patients understand why they may need glasses/contact lenses after surgery. Excimer laser ablation to correct hyeropia after endothelial keratoplasty may be judiciously considered after sufficient healing time has occurred.

question: Which of the following indications is the only one acceptable for a conjunctival flap (Gundersen)?

options.C: persistent epithelial defect in a poor visual potential eye

explanation: A Gundersen flap involves incising and then rotating a piece of conjunctiva so that it covers the cornea. Because post operative examination of the cornea is affected by the overlying conjunctiva, it should not be done in cases where a detailed exam of the underlying cornea needs to be performed.

question: Which of the following is associated with mitomycin C (MMC) use?
explanation: Mitomycin C (MMC) is an antibiotic/anti-metabolite that is produced by the actinobacterium, Streptomyces caespitosus. It is used for a broad number of reasons in Ophthalmology including: preventing pterygium recurrence, decreasing fibrosis after glaucoma filtering surgery, for the treatment of conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia, and to prevent haze after photorefractive keratectomy. Non-healing corneal epithelial defects and infectious sclerokeratitis are potential complications of MMC use with the most dreaded complication being scleral melt/necrosis. Infectious sclerokeratitis occurs because the eye is placed into a reduced immune level and superinfection can occur. It prevents fibrosis (scarring) and thus can lead to hypotony after trabeculectomy.

question: Which of the following diseases is least likely to be definitely diagnosed with a conjunctival biopsy (assuming an appropriate clinical context)?
explanation: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem idiopathic inflammatory condition that can cause granulomatous inflammation in the conjunctiva. Any conjunctival nodule or follicle in a patient with clinical signs of sarcoid should be biopsied because it may spare the patient a more invasive biopsy (for instance a bronchoscopy with biopsy). Mucous membrane pemphigoid (formerly known as ocular cicatricial pemphigoid) is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory condition of the orofacial membranes and can result in severe conjunctival scarring with symblepharon formation. Diagnosis may be made on conjunctival biopsy with immunofluorescent staining that would show C3, IgG, IgM, and/or IgA deposition along the basement membrane zone of the epithelium. Batten disease is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative disorder that begins in childhood and belongs to the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis family of diseases. It results in accumulation of lipopigments in lysozomes throughout the body due to a defect in lipopigment metabolism. The lipopigments do deposit in the conjunctiva (among many other places such as skin) and a conjunctival biopsy can confirm the diagnosis. The use of a conjunctival biopsy has not been reported to confirm a diagnosis of choroideremia, which causes diffuse and progressive degeneration of the RPE and choriocapillaris.

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the clinical finding shown in these slit-lamp photographs?

options.A: This entity follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern
options.B: If detected in a middle age patient, surgical intervention should proceed with minimal delay in order to decrease long-term vision loss
options.C: Patients usually report worse visual symptoms with mesopic or scotopic light conditions
options.D: Hydrodissection should be avoided during surgical intervention

explanation: The slit-lamp photographs show a posterior polar cataract with slit-beam illumination and retroillumination. Posterior polar cataracts (PPCs) are a rare form of cataract that have a unique clinical appearance. PPCs are thought to arise from a remnant of the fetal hyaloid artery, which in benign cases can cause the commonly seen Mittendorf dot and in more progressive cases, can cause a clinically significant cataract. PPCs usually develop early in life with varying amounts of clinical significance. In children, they may cause significant, profound vision loss that may necessitate early surgical intervention, or they may cause minimal/no vision changes, and therefore may not be detected until later in life. They usually occur bilaterally. PPCs are thought to have an autosomal dominant nheritance pattern, though multiple genes have been implicated and described in the literature. An autosomal recessive (choice A) inheritance pattern has not been described to date. Different classification schemes have been reported in the literature revolving around their phenotypic appearance and/or clinical relevance. In general, if noted to be causing minimal/no vision changes, observation and conservative management with glasses/contact lenses may be a reasonable option (choice B). An interesting finding with PPCs is that given their location is usually in the center of lens (and therefore it may obstruct the visual axis), vision may be worse under photopic (bright light) conditions when the pupil is smaller, and vision may be better under mesopic/scotopic (dim light) conditions when the pupil is larger and the patient is able to "look around" the cataract (choice C). Surgical management of PPCs may be challenging to the novice surgeon, and careful consideration must be given to management of these cataracts. In general, because the PPCs anatomy is such that usually the PPC is fused to the posterior capsule, cataract surgery in this setting is associated with increased risk of posterior capsule breaks, vitreous loss and other associated complications. The literature describes a plethora of surgical considerations during cataract extraction of PPCs, but most experts are in agreement that while partial hydrodissection is possible, it is advisable to avoid hydrodissection (choice D) and instead perform hydrodelineation in order to avoid disruption of the PPC and posterior capsule adhesions. Multiple strategies, including the "inside-out" and "reverse flower bloom" techniques, have been described and videos of these are readily available online. In addition to knowing this for the test, you should watch these videos and learn these strategies for your clinical practice in the future! Extra: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qZq8bJsZYAA.
